items.title: DeepMind's AlphaProof Code uses AI agents to formally verify Signal's encryption code
items.tldr: Google DeepMind used a team of AI agents to produce machine-checked mathematical proofs that the compiled code behind Signal's messaging protocol keeps key security promises.
items.summary_md: Formal verification means proving, with the rigor of a math proof, that software behaves as specified; here the proofs are written in Lean, a proof language whose checker rejects any flawed step. Human experts wrote the security specifications, and Gemini-powered agents did the proving in about four weeks, flagging roughly 1% of the code for human review. As a test, the team put two old, already-fixed bugs back into an isolated copy of the code, and the system proved both versions insecure. These are DeepMind's own claims; it is releasing the proof files and a technical paper, but not saying whether the agent framework itself will be public.

items.title: Linux Foundation takes on Agent Name Service, a DNS-based ID system for AI agents
items.tldr: An open standard that lets AI agents prove who they are, using the same domain-name system and certificates that websites already rely on, is now a neutral Linux Foundation project.
items.summary_md: Agent Name Service (ANS) ties each agent's name to a web domain, publishes its identity through DNS (the internet's address book), and lets other agents check it with standard web certificates before trusting it. It also watches identity records for unauthorized changes. Eleven organizations, including Cisco, Cloudflare, GoDaddy, Salesforce and OWASP, have contributed to or adopted it since it was first proposed in June. The seven-document specification is now run by an open technical steering committee.

items.title: Microsoft researchers show an AI agent can be backdoored by editing fewer than 10 neurons
items.tldr: Microsoft Research showed that an attacker who can change a model's stored weights could plant a hidden trigger that makes an otherwise normal agent run malicious code.
items.summary_md: The technique, called Lazarus, rewires a handful of rarely used "dormant" neurons so they fire only when a trigger appears, such as the system clock passing into 2027, and then make the agent download and run attacker code mid-task. It needs no retraining, only about 50 examples and ordinary computing power, so anyone with write access to a model file could do it, and the model still passes normal safety tests. Microsoft urges checking where models come from, comparing weights against the official version, limiting agent permissions and reviewing high-stakes actions before they run.

items.title: Databricks relaunches Genie as an always-on agent that works in the background
items.tldr: Databricks' second-generation Genie takes a goal, splits the work among helper agents, and contacts people only when it needs a decision.
items.summary_md: Genie now runs on its own computing resources and reports through a priority inbox, with each new alert arriving as an unread email. It can search company data and apps such as Google Drive, Jira and Confluence, and keeps an "ontology", a living map of a company's terms, metrics, people and processes. It only sees what each user is allowed to see, admins can set approval rules and spending limits, and every action is logged. The core Genie is available now, while the always-on mode and search are still coming to preview; pricing is per use, with no figures given.

items.title: Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 hits 96% in a Mercedes-Benz factory pilot
items.tldr: DeepMind's newest robot-control model is more dexterous, faster and safer than earlier versions, and handled real car-factory work in a trial.
items.summary_md: Gemini Robotics 2.5 is a vision-language-action model: it takes in camera images and instructions and outputs robot movements. Across more than 200 tasks, DeepMind reports 30% to 100% higher success than earlier baselines and 20% to 30% faster completion. On Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid at two Mercedes-Benz plants, it picked metal brackets from bins into per-car trays with a 96% success rate in a proof-of-concept. It is rolling out only to DeepMind's robotics partners for now.

items.title: AlphaGenome 2 predicts how DNA changes act in specific cell types
items.tldr: Google DeepMind's upgraded DNA model can now be told which cell type or state to consider, and it found about twice as many disease-causing variants as its predecessor in a benchmark.
items.summary_md: A genetic variant is a single change in the DNA letters, and most disease-linked variants alter how strongly nearby genes are switched on rather than changing a protein. Across 28 immune cell types, AlphaGenome 2 picked out 30% of known causal variants versus 16% for the original model, and got the direction of the effect (more or less gene activity) right 43% of the time versus 23%. It was trained on more than 107 million single-cell profiles and can take a researcher's own single-cell data. It is free for non-commercial research through an API, is not cleared for clinical use, and its predictions still need lab confirmation.

items.title: ElevenLabs releases Scribe v3 speech-to-text models
items.tldr: ElevenLabs' new transcription models make 27% fewer word errors than the previous version across 102 languages, and the live version now labels who is speaking.
items.summary_md: Scribe v3 handles recorded audio, while Scribe v3 Live works in real time with lower delay. ElevenLabs reports 17% fewer speaker-labeling errors on recordings with three or more people, and a 3.1% speaker-labeling error rate for v3 Live in English, versus 5.9% to 7.3% for other real-time models it tested. Users can supply up to 1,000 key terms, such as drug or product names, to improve accuracy. A version of Scribe v3 Live tuned for medical conversations is also being released for the company's agent platform; no pricing changes were stated.

items.title: Alibaba opens a preview of its flagship Qwen4-Max model
items.tldr: Alibaba gave developers early access to Qwen4-Max, the top model in its next Qwen family, which can read about a million tokens at once and accepts images and video.
items.summary_md: A token is a chunk of text of about three-quarters of a word, so a million-token context window is roughly several long books in one prompt. Developers can reach the preview through Alibaba's Token Plan subscription, and it is also in the Qwen app and Alibaba's coding and work tools such as Qoder and QwenWork. TechNode's report gives no benchmark scores or prices, so how it compares with Western frontier models is not yet clear.

items.title: A non-archaeologist's 48 AI agents found a hidden Maya site, then learned scientists got there first
items.tldr: A hobbyist had 48 AI agents scan public NASA lidar maps of the Maya region overnight and they spotted an apparent jungle-covered settlement, which turned out to be already described in a 2025 study.
items.summary_md: Lidar is a laser-scanning method that maps the ground beneath forest canopy. The agents screened about 1,200 square kilometers of images, ruled out hills and sinkholes, and flagged a hilltop site with an apparent plaza, an oval pyramid and a possible reservoir. Mexico's archaeology institute replied it had no registered site there, but in a Nov. 11 update the author found the agents had missed a 2025 journal paper that already documented it. He now calls it a rediscovery, and still argues curious outsiders with AI agents can do real research.

items.title: AI-generated cats and pigs turn Chinese creators into online stars
items.tldr: Short videos of AI-made animals acting out little stories are drawing millions of views in China and paying their creators through brand deals.
items.summary_md: One former real-estate planner's orange-and-white AI cats have more than 92 million views across 92 Bilibili clips, including one where a cat tumbles into a river while fishing. A designer whose cat began as an accidental image of a cat on her carpet now earns more from about two ad campaigns a month than from her day job. On Douyin, China's TikTok, the "AI pets" hashtag has over 3.1 billion views. Creators say people reposting their work without permission is a constant headache.

items.title: A humanoid robot entered an Antarctic ultra-marathon and ran 3 km before its battery froze
items.tldr: A humanoid robot called Qestr lined up with 25 human runners at the Antarctic Ice Ultra but dropped out after about 3 km when the -24°C cold drained its battery.
items.summary_md: Qestr was the first humanoid robot to enter the race, held near Ultima Camp in Antarctica on Nov. 8, and wore a custom thermal jacket. Its running looked steady at first, but lithium-ion batteries lose power fast in deep cold, so it withdrew without an official time. The race report blames the battery, not the ice or terrain, for the early exit.

sections.name: AI in Cardiac Surgery, Robotics & AI Models

items.title: Smartwatch ECG plus AI flags weak heart pumping, and repeat recordings cut false alarms
items.source: American Heart Association Newsroom (AHA Scientific Sessions 2026)
items.tldr: A Korean study at AHA 2026 found an AI model reading 30-second smartwatch ECGs could spot a weakly pumping left ventricle, and requiring positive results on 2 of 3 days halved false alarms.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
A late-breaking abstract at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 tested an AI model that reads single-lead smartwatch ECGs to detect left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD). LVSD means the main pumping chamber squeezes weakly, defined here as an ejection fraction of 40% or less. Each AI result was checked against an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) at one South Korean hospital.

## Why it matters
LVSD often goes unnoticed until heart failure symptoms appear, and echo is not a screening test. Millions of people already wear watches that record an ECG. If a cheap home recording could flag who needs an echo, screening could reach far more people.

## Key details
- In the clinic group, 2,211 adults recorded back-to-back on an Apple Watch and a Samsung Galaxy Watch. The model worked about equally well on both, but 200 people (9%) were positive on one watch and negative on the other.
- In the home group, 146 patients recorded on their own watches for a week, and 108 recorded on at least five days.
- Calling someone positive after one positive day caught 33 of 38 LVSD cases, with 18 false positives among 70 people without LVSD.
- Requiring 2 of 3 consecutive positive days caught 31 of 38 cases, with only 9 false positives. By my arithmetic from these counts, that moves specificity from about 74% to about 87% at a small cost in sensitivity.
- The lead author is chief medical officer of Medical AI Co., which built the model.

## Caveats
This is an abstract, not a peer-reviewed paper. It comes from one hospital, and participants were already referred for echo, so LVSD was far more common than in the general public. The repeat-testing rule was one of several examined in a small exploratory subgroup. The release gives no AUC for the clinic comparison. The study did not test whether earlier detection improves outcomes.

## Key terms
- **LVSD**: left ventricular systolic dysfunction, a weak squeeze of the heart's main pumping chamber.
- **Ejection fraction**: the share of blood the left ventricle pushes out with each beat; about 55-70% is normal.
- **Single-lead ECG**: a heart rhythm trace from one electrical viewpoint, as a watch records, versus 12 in a hospital ECG.
- **Sensitivity / specificity**: the share of sick people correctly flagged / the share of healthy people correctly cleared.

items.title: Nurses with AI guidance captured research-quality heart ultrasounds for 4,597 rural adults
items.source: American Heart Association Newsroom (AHA Scientific Sessions 2026)
items.tldr: In a Duke-led mobile clinic study, non-sonographers using real-time AI guidance produced complete, measurable echocardiograms in 98% of scans, with a median scan time of 9.5 minutes.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
A poster at AHA Scientific Sessions 2026 reported how echocardiograms were collected in the RURAL study, a Duke-led cohort on heart and lung health in rural America. A mobile health unit visited 10 rural counties in Alabama, Kentucky, Louisiana and Mississippi from November 2021 to June 2026. The scans were not done by sonographers. Fourteen nurses, nursing assistants and CT technicians took a 2-hour training course and then scanned with software that coached them in real time. Experts at the Duke Clinical Research Institute imaging core lab reviewed every study remotely.

## Why it matters
Many rural areas have few sonographers, so people there rarely get an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) until they are already sick. This study shows that AI-guided acquisition plus remote expert review can produce research-grade images at scale. Unlike AI tools that read finished scans, this one helps a novice capture the images in the first place.

## Key details
- 4,597 adults aged 25-65 were scanned (average age 48, 67% women, 35% Black).
- 98% of scans contained all six required standard views, and more than 99% were adequate for measurements.
- Diagnostic quality for individual views ranged from 77% to 94%.
- Median scan time was 9.5 minutes, and 81% finished within the 15-minute target.
- 133 scans had critical findings, most often an ejection fraction below 50%. In 99% of these cases, results reached participants within three days.
- Three of the 14 operators needed retraining after their first scans were reviewed.

## Caveats
These are preliminary, non-peer-reviewed data. There was no head-to-head comparison with scans by trained sonographers. Only one AI software brand and one core lab were used, and the release does not name the product. Differences between operators scanning the same person were not systematically measured. The study did not test whether returning results changed care or health.

## Key terms
- **Echocardiogram**: an ultrasound movie of the heart used to measure its size and pumping.
- **AI-guided acquisition**: software that tells the operator how to move the probe to get a correct view.
- **Standard views**: set probe positions that show the heart from defined angles so measurements are comparable.
- **Core lab**: a central expert team that reads and quality-checks images from many sites in a uniform way.

items.title: A Unified Framework for Comprehensive Cardiac CT Segmentation and Phenotyping
items.tldr: A Bern-led team built a 1,598-scan expert-labelled cardiac CT dataset and a foundation model pre-trained on 60,000 unlabelled scans that segments 14 heart structures better than existing open-source tools.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Researchers led by teams in Bern, Switzerland, posted a paper describing a full pipeline for cardiac CT segmentation. Segmentation means outlining each structure in a 3D scan, voxel by voxel. They assembled 1,598 cardiac CT scans with expert outlines of 14 cardiac structures. They used 1,000 for training and kept 598 for external testing. They also pre-trained a model on 60,000 unlabelled cardiac CT scans. They say they will release the dataset, code, model weights, augmentation library and software openly.

## Why it matters
Good cardiac CT models are limited mostly by labelled data, because expert outlining is slow and costly. A large, multi-structure, openly released dataset gives the field a shared benchmark and training base. The finding that different network designs performed about the same suggests effort is better spent on data quality and pre-training than on new architectures.

## How it works
- **Human-in-the-loop annotation**: a model drafts the outlines and experts correct them, which speeds up labelling.
- **Self-supervised pre-training**: the model first learns general CT anatomy from 60,000 scans without labels, then is fine-tuned on the labelled set. This helped most when few labels were available.
- **Architecture comparison**: convolutional, transformer and state-space networks were tested and gave similar accuracy.
- **Evaluation**: tested on five external datasets, where it beat existing open-source tools.
- **Phenotyping**: volumes and shapes from the outlines carried information on ventricular function and disease severity beyond age and sex.

## Caveats
This is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed. The abstract gives no per-structure accuracy numbers. The training scans come from the public ImageCAS coronary CT angiography set. The Hugging Face dataset page carries a non-commercial, no-derivatives licence. It also says full public release waits for journal acceptance. The phenotyping results are associations, not proof of clinical benefit.

## Key terms
- **Foundation model**: a large model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks.
- **Self-supervised learning**: training on unlabelled data by having the model solve tasks it sets itself, such as filling in hidden parts of an image.
- **External testing**: checking a model on data from hospitals or scanners it never saw in training.
- **Phenotyping**: turning images into measurable traits, such as chamber volumes, to describe a patient's disease.
- **State-space model**: a newer network type that processes long sequences efficiently, an alternative to transformers.

items.title: Patients' AI agents are coming for appointment scheduling. Should health systems let them in?
items.tldr: Emory Healthcare's chief AI officer says consumer AI agents from frontier labs already send scheduling traffic to health systems, which now must decide whether to block them, let them in, or build their own.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Becker's Hospital Review spoke with Nabile Safdar, MD, chief AI officer at Emory Healthcare in Atlanta. He said personal AI agents are starting to book care for patients. Frontier AI labs whose apps link to medical records began sending this kind of traffic to health systems this summer. The story ran on November 10, 2026, after Becker's CEO + CFO Roundtable in Chicago.

## Why it matters
Scheduling is one of the most staff-heavy parts of running a hospital. Until now, the health system controlled every booking channel: phone, patient portal, or its own chatbot. Outside agents change that. A patient's own assistant may now request, move or cancel appointments. Hospitals must set rules for traffic they did not design and cannot fully check.

## Key details
- Consumer tools named include OpenAI's ChatGPT Health, which links US provider records, and Anthropic's Claude, which accepts uploaded lab results and records. Safdar also expects agents from Meta and X.
- Epic, the largest hospital electronic health record (EHR) vendor, already offers AI self-scheduling to its customers.
- Safdar sees two paths. Health systems can block outside agents, as some banks do for agent-made transactions. Or they can build their own highly automated scheduling.
- He warned that patients carry much of the risk when an outside agent acts for them. He called it a case of buyer beware.
- He also raised equity. Many patients do not know what these agents are. Agent-based booking could mostly help people who already have the best access to care.

## Caveats
This is one executive's view from a conference interview. The article gives no traffic volumes, error rates or booking numbers. It does not say how Emory currently handles agent requests. Rules on identity checks and liability for wrong bookings are still open questions.

## Key terms
- **AI agent:** software that can take actions for a user, such as filling forms or booking slots, not just answer questions.
- **Frontier lab:** a company building the most capable general AI models, such as OpenAI or Anthropic.
- **EHR (electronic health record):** the hospital's main digital system for patient charts, orders and schedules.
- **Self-scheduling:** letting patients book appointments directly without calling staff.
- **Health equity:** fair access to care across income, language and digital-skill groups.

items.title: Akara raises $5.5M to bring privacy-preserving AI to hospitals
items.tldr: Irish start-up Akara raised $5.5 million for wall-mounted thermal sensors and on-device AI that track how hospital rooms are used, without capturing detailed images of patients or staff.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Akara, a spin-out from Trinity College Dublin, announced $5.5 million in new funding on November 11, 2026. Its total funding is now $12.3 million. Locke Health led the round. VTC Ventures, the EIC Fund, CommonKind and NovaVector Holdings joined, along with earlier backers ACT, Atlantic Bridge and Enterprise Ireland. The company builds AI to track and coordinate how hospital spaces are used.

## Why it matters
Operating rooms and procedure rooms are some of a hospital's most expensive assets. Knowing when a room is empty, being cleaned or ready is key to turnover and patient flow. Much of this status is still logged by hand. Camera systems can automate it, but raise privacy worries for patients and staff. Akara's pitch is automation without identifiable video. The release cites a claim that over 40% of US hospitals run at a loss, so efficiency tools draw interest.

## Key details
- **Sensors:** wall-mounted units use thermal sensing, which reads heat patterns rather than ordinary pictures, so people are not shown in detail.
- **Edge AI:** the analysis runs on each device. Less sensitive data leaves the room, and less IT infrastructure is needed.
- **Event detection:** software spots key moments in a room and alerts staff. The company compares it to an air traffic controller.
- **AI agents:** staff can ask questions about room-use data in plain language and generate reports.
- **Deployments:** the system is already in some US ambulatory surgery centers and hospitals. No sites are named.
- **Use of funds:** larger engineering and operations teams, faster adoption, and AI agents for more uses.

## Caveats
This is a company press release. It reports no measured results, such as minutes saved per room turnover or added cases per day. It names no customers and gives no deployment count. Thermal data still describe staff activity, so workplace-monitoring and labour questions remain even without images.

## Key terms
- **Thermal sensing:** detecting body heat and movement as temperature patterns instead of camera images.
- **Edge AI:** running AI on the device itself rather than sending raw data to a central server or cloud.
- **Room turnover:** the time between one procedure ending and the room being ready for the next.
- **Ambulatory surgery center:** an outpatient facility for same-day surgical procedures.

items.title: Capacity Planning for Resource-Constrained Clinical LLM Serving
items.tldr: A Weill Cornell study finds that, for a hospital running its own language models on four GPUs, the mix of small and large models matters far more for speed and coverage than the rules used to route requests between them.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Researchers at Weill Cornell Medicine and Cornell University posted a study on October 31, 2026. They asked a practical question for health systems that host AI in-house. With a fixed budget of four GPUs, how many should run a small language model and how many a large one? And how should incoming requests be routed?

## Why it matters
Many hospitals want to run large language models (LLMs) on their own hardware to keep patient data in-house. GPUs are scarce and costly. Poor setup means slow answers for clinicians or missed content in summaries.

## How it works
- Each GPU (NVIDIA A100, 80 GB) ran one model through vLLM, an open-source serving engine. The small model was Qwen2.5-7B and the large one Qwen2.5-14B.
- They tested four fleets: four small, three small plus one large, two plus two, and four large.
- Each run sent 240 requests from three public tasks: health claim checking (PubHealth), biomedical sentence similarity (BioSSES), and hospital course summaries from MIMIC, a de-identified ICU record database.
- They compared several routing policies under normal and overload traffic, across 24 setups.
- Fleet mix explained about 65% of the variation in average latency, versus about 13% for routing.
- All-small fleets answered fastest: about 0.11 s to the first word and 2.6 s on average. But they covered less of the long summaries.
- With one large model among three small ones, that single large GPU became a bottleneck, with p95 latency near 23.6 s.
- A capacity-aware router cut average latency by 11–13% and raised throughput by 13–17% in that setup, with a small loss in summary coverage.

## Caveats
Summary quality was scored by word overlap, not by clinicians, so safety and hallucinations were not checked. One model family and one GPU type were tested, on simulated traffic. Most setups were run once. Cost, security and EHR integration were not studied.

## Key terms
- **GPU:** a graphics processor used to run AI models fast; the main hardware cost of hosting LLMs.
- **Routing policy:** the rule that decides which model copy handles each incoming request.
- **Latency / p95 latency:** response time; p95 is the time within which 95% of requests finish.
- **Throughput:** how many requests the system completes per second.
- **Token recall:** share of words in a reference summary that also appear in the model's summary.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in FDA regulatory correspondence, 2022 to 2026: a retrospective document analysis
items.tldr: A search of 3,011 FDA warning letters from 2022 to September 2026 found only seven that mention AI, and just one that treats a company's own AI use as a violation.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Two authors searched the full text of every FDA warning letter posted between January 2022 and 28 September 2026, 3,011 letters in all, for references to artificial intelligence. Only 7 letters (0.23%) qualified. Three involved medical devices, three involved e-cigarette products and one involved drug manufacturing. The paper was published on 31 October 2026.

## Why it matters
There is a lot of talk about the FDA "cracking down" on AI in regulated industry. This study gives a hard count. AI is not a new category of enforcement: when the FDA does mention it, it applies rules that already exist. The single drug case, the April 2026 letter to Purolea Cosmetics Lab, cited 21 CFR 211.22(c) because the quality unit did not properly review manufacturing documents that AI had generated. For anyone using AI to draft batch records or specifications, the message is that human sign-off is the legal duty, not the tool.

## How it works
The authors ran keyword searches on the letters, then removed false hits, such as "AI" meaning adequate intake. For each remaining letter they recorded where AI appeared, how it related to the product or process, and which violations were cited. In all seven letters AI sat alongside other violations (36 in total), never alone. They also looked at three inspection records released under freedom-of-information requests that mention AI; none treated AI use as a deficiency.

## Caveats
The counts are small, so they cannot show a trend. Keyword searches miss wording like "automated algorithm". One author did the screening, helped by a large language model, with no second reviewer. Warning letters reflect which cases the FDA chooses to pursue, not how much industry uses AI. Both authors work for KeyPedia, a company that sells regulatory data products, which the paper discloses.

## Key terms
- **Warning letter:** a public FDA notice telling a company it has significantly broken the law and must fix it.
- **Quality unit:** the group in a drug plant legally responsible for approving or rejecting procedures, records and batches.
- **21 CFR 211:** the US current good manufacturing practice (cGMP) rules for finished drugs.
- **Form 483:** the list of observations an FDA inspector hands over at the end of an inspection.
- **Retrospective document analysis:** a study that reviews existing records rather than collecting new data.

items.title: GC Biopharma builds generative AI tool to screen research papers for drug safety cases
items.tldr: South Korean drugmaker GC Biopharma has built an in-house generative AI tool that reads published papers and flags which ones contain reportable side-effect cases for its products.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
GC Biopharma announced PVLitrieve, generative AI software it built itself to handle part of pharmacovigilance literature review. Staff feed it a list of research papers and conference abstracts. The tool reads each one, decides whether it contains safety information about a company product, and judges whether that information meets the bar for a reportable case. The company says it is the first Korean drugmaker to build such a tool in-house.

## Why it matters
Drug companies must regularly search the medical literature for side effects of their products and report qualifying cases to regulators. This is slow, repetitive work, and missing a case is a compliance failure. A tool that safely removes irrelevant papers frees safety staff for real assessment. The design choice of keeping a human as the final decision-maker matches what regulators such as the FDA and EMA expect for AI in safety work.

## Key details
- A case is reportable only when four elements are present: an identifiable reporter, an identifiable patient, a suspected medicine and an adverse event.
- The tool writes its verdict and its reasoning into an Excel file, and a pharmacovigilance specialist makes the final call.
- In initial validation on about 600 papers, negative predictive value was 100%: every paper the AI labelled "not applicable" was also judged not applicable by experts.
- In 2027 the company plans to add literature searching and draft report writing, to cover the whole literature monitoring process.

## Caveats
This is a company announcement reported by a newspaper, not a peer-reviewed study. Only one performance figure was released. A 100% negative predictive value on 600 papers is encouraging for safety, since it means no relevant paper was wrongly discarded in that set, but no sensitivity, false-positive rate or time-saving figures were given. Results may differ on other products or languages, and no regulator has reviewed the tool.

## Key terms
- **Pharmacovigilance:** monitoring, assessing and reporting the side effects of medicines after (and before) approval.
- **Literature monitoring:** the required routine search of published papers for side-effect reports about a company's products.
- **Individual case safety report (ICSR):** a formal report of one patient's suspected side effect, sent to regulators.
- **Negative predictive value:** of all items a test calls negative, the share that are truly negative.
- **Generative AI:** AI models that produce text or other content, such as large language models.

items.title: What eight Asia-Pacific regulators have actually published on AI in drug development
items.tldr: A document-by-document review finds that none of eight major Asia-Pacific drug regulators has a final guideline telling sponsors how to use AI in drug development.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
BioPharma APAC checked the official output of eight Asia-Pacific regulators, with a data cut-off of 21 October 2026, to see what each has really published on AI in drug development. The answer: no final guideline aimed at drug sponsors exists in any of them. South Korea's MFDS is the only one to have consulted on a draft (June 2024), and its final document is scheduled for release on 15 December 2026.

## Why it matters
Much attention goes to the FDA and EMA, but companies running trials or filing in Asia need to know what local regulators expect. The review separates real documents from speeches and rumours. It shows that sponsors in the region will mostly lean on shared international texts and on FDA and EMA thinking for now.

## Key details
- **Japan (PMDA):** has an internal AI action plan (October 2025); a broader "basic approach" is targeted by 31 March 2027.
- **China (NMPA):** an April 2026 policy on AI in drug regulation mainly covers the agency's own use and promises industry principles not yet published.
- **Singapore (HSA):** statements and an HSA-MHRA collaboration, but no public draft.
- **India (CDSCO):** an AI expert committee was announced orally in September 2026, with no published terms. Pages describing a CDSCO AI validation framework could not be traced to CDSCO's site.
- **Australia, Taiwan:** AI guidance exists for medical devices only. **Malaysia:** nothing found.
- **ICH M15**, adopted 29 January 2026, is the only common text. It covers AI and machine learning used to generate model-informed drug development evidence.
- Scope differs: the FDA draft excludes drug discovery, while EMA's reflection paper covers the whole medicine lifecycle.

## Caveats
This is an analysis article without a named author. It reflects what was findable online by the cut-off date, so documents in local languages or not yet posted may be missed. It describes publication status, not how strictly each regulator reviews AI in practice.

## Key terms
- **Sponsor:** the company or organisation responsible for a clinical trial or marketing application.
- **ICH:** the International Council for Harmonisation, which writes technical drug guidelines shared by major regulators.
- **Model-informed drug development (MIDD):** using mathematical and computer models to guide dosing, trial design and regulatory decisions.
- **Reflection paper:** an EMA document setting out current thinking on a topic, less binding than a guideline.
- **MFDS:** Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety, the national medicines regulator.

items.title: FDA asks for feedback on autonomous and remotely operated robotic medical devices
items.source: U.S. FDA, Center for Devices and Radiological Health
items.tldr: The FDA released a discussion paper on how to weigh the benefits and risks of robotic devices that act on their own or are controlled from far away, and wants comments by January 5, 2027.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
On November 6, 2026, the FDA's device center (CDRH) posted a discussion paper titled *Evaluating Benefit-Risk in Robotic Medical Devices with Autonomous or Remote Teleoperation Capabilities*. It asks the public for feedback. The paper covers robots that do diagnostic, therapeutic or rehabilitation tasks on the body. That includes surgery and non-surgical jobs such as positioning an imaging probe. Comments go to docket FDA-2026-N-13135 until January 5, 2027. A hybrid public workshop on the same topics runs December 2–3, 2026, at the FDA's White Oak campus and by webcast.

## Why it matters
This is the FDA's first structured look at robots that act with some independence or are steered from another site. As of July, MedTech Dive reports, no remotely teleoperated or fully autonomous robotic device had US marketing authorization. Autonomy in practice usually means software, often machine learning, making movement decisions. So the ideas in this paper will likely shape how AI-driven robots are reviewed later. A September draft guidance on surgical robots deliberately left these two categories out.

## Key details
- The paper is organized around four topics: terminology, benefit-risk for autonomous functions, benefit-risk for remote teleoperation, and risk mitigations.
- The FDA says these features could widen access to specialist care and make procedures more consistent.
- MedTech Dive reports the risks the FDA names: the robot carrying out a step wrongly, users paying less attention, and poor handling of unusual anatomy or procedures.
- Workshop day 1 covers patients, autonomy, teleoperation, health-system readiness and reimbursement. Day 2 covers risk management, cybersecurity and infrastructure.

## Caveats
The FDA says the paper is for discussion only. It is not draft or final guidance and does not change policy. The public web page does not spell out levels of autonomy or the exact questions. Those are in the full PDF, which this summary did not review.

## Key terms
- **Teleoperation**: a clinician controls the robot from a different location over a network.
- **Autonomous function**: the device carries out part of a task without moment-to-moment human control.
- **Benefit-risk assessment**: the FDA's weighing of a device's likely benefits against its likely harms.
- **Docket**: the public file on Regulations.gov where comments on an FDA document are submitted.
- **Discussion paper**: an early FDA document that asks questions; it carries no regulatory weight.

items.title: FDA AI-enabled device authorizations rose 160% from 2021 to 2025, with radiology dominant (preprint)
items.tldr: A new cross-sectional count of the FDA's AI-enabled device list finds 1,087 authorizations from 2021 to 2025: 79% were in radiology and 97% came through the 510(k) pathway.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Malik Muhammad Makki and Samia Yunas posted a preprint on Research Square on November 10, 2026. They analyzed the FDA's public list of AI-enabled medical devices, which they accessed on November 6, 2026. They grouped each unique submission by the year of the final decision, the lead review panel and the regulatory pathway. Their main window was 2021–2025. They report decisions from 2026 (through June 29) separately.

## Why it matters
The FDA list is the main public record of which AI devices are on the US market. Counts by year, specialty and pathway show where AI is entering care and how lightly it is reviewed. Annual authorizations went from 129 in 2021 to 335 in 2025, an increase of about 160%. Another 181 came in the first half of 2026 alone. Nearly all used 510(k), the pathway that compares a device with one already on the market. That pathway usually does not require new clinical trials. The authors stress that FDA authorization sets a legal baseline. Showing lasting patient benefit takes separate evidence.

## How it works
- **Data**: the FDA's AI-enabled device list, deduplicated by submission number.
- **Cohort**: 1,087 records for 2021–2025 (129, 162, 226, 235 and 335 per year).
- **Specialty**: radiology 863 (79.4%), cardiovascular 91 (8.4%), neurology 50 (4.6%).
- **Pathway**: 510(k) 1,055 (97.1%), De Novo 24 (2.2%), premarket approval 8 (0.7%).
- The authors also used selected clinical studies to describe what the devices do in practice. They say these uses are narrow, such as detecting findings and supporting diagnostic workflow.

## Caveats
This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Only the abstract is shown on the landing page. The page gives no methods for choosing the clinical studies and lists no limitations. The FDA list depends on how the agency tags AI. Counting authorizations says nothing about uptake, performance or safety after launch.

## Key terms
- **510(k)**: an FDA pathway that clears a device by showing it is "substantially equivalent" to a legally marketed predicate device.
- **De Novo**: the pathway for new low-to-moderate-risk devices with no predicate.
- **Premarket approval (PMA)**: the strictest pathway, for high-risk devices, usually needing clinical data.
- **Lead panel**: the FDA medical-specialty group mainly responsible for reviewing a device.
- **Preprint**: a study shared publicly before peer review.

items.title: Health Canada AI licence for DIAGNOS retinal tool came 40 days after a meeting that took 15 months to get
items.tldr: DIAGNOS's CEO says its AI retinal-analysis software got a Class II Health Canada licence 40 days after a face-to-face meeting with reviewers, but that meeting took about 15 months to get.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Startup Fortune interviewed André Larente, CEO of DIAGNOS, a company based in Brossard, Quebec. DIAGNOS makes CARA, an AI system that analyzes fundus photos (photos of the back of the eye) for optometrists. CARA received a Health Canada Medical Device Licence on July 23, 2026. The article reports it as Class II. Larente said Health Canada's published review timelines were not met. It took about 15 months to get an in-person meeting about the submission's risks. The licence was issued 40 days after that meeting.

## Why it matters
This is a rare inside view of how an AI device moves through Health Canada's review. The bottleneck was not the technology. It was getting a chance to explain the intended use and risk in person. The company brought the director of a Montreal optometry school to describe how optometrists would actually use the tool. For developers, this suggests that clinical context matters. A clear intended-use statement, backed by a clinician who can describe the workflow, may speed up review of software as a medical device.

## Key details
- CARA's modules screen for age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy, analyze small retinal blood vessels and enhance retinal images.
- The optometrist keeps control of every clinical decision. The tool supports clinicians and does not diagnose on its own.
- The licence lets DIAGNOS serve IRIS The Visual Group and the wider Canadian optometry market.
- The company also holds Saudi authorization and names a US pathway as a strategic priority.

## Caveats
This account is the company's view, given in an interview. Health Canada has not commented on the timeline. The article reports no accuracy figures such as sensitivity or specificity. The "500,000 images analyzed" figure reflects usage, not validated performance. The licence itself dates from July.

## Key terms
- **Medical Device Licence (MDL)**: Health Canada's market authorization, required for Class II–IV devices.
- **Class II**: Canada's lower-moderate risk class; the application relies mainly on the manufacturer's declarations and evidence summaries.
- **Fundus image**: a photo of the retina and optic nerve at the back of the eye.
- **Intended use**: the manufacturer's statement of what the device is for and who uses it, which drives its risk class.
- **Software as a medical device (SaMD)**: software that performs a medical function by itself, without being part of hardware.
